narrative: Statutory civil remedy under PC § 290.46(j)(4)(A): actual damages, up to treble and not less than $250, plus attorney's fees and exemplary damages, or a civil penalty not exceeding $25,000 — the $25,000 figure is a cap on the civil penalty, not a floor alternative to actual damages. CONSERVATIVE: civil-penalty cap plus modest actuals/emotional distress (no W-2; never hired). MODERATE: ~$85,000 (actuals/treble, ICRAA, emotional distress, fee-shifting). AGGRESSIVE: ~$200,000 if discovery confirms willful registry-based denial and supports Civil Code § 3294 punitives. UPS Exhibit A is now in the record; Dkt. 14 admits NSOR-based employment use. The remaining fight is statutory construction and source, not whether the report exists or was used.
risk: Merits posture unchanged by removal — a federal court sitting in diversity applies the same California substantive law. PC §290.46(j)(2)(E) still bars employment use. Dkt. 14 (filed Sep. 14) walks back ECF 7's 'not a single reference to any California based sex offender registry' and admits NSOR was searched, Record Found, and 'when UPS learned that Plaintiff was included on the National Sex Offender Registry, it used that information when making its employment decisions related to Plaintiff.' Use of sex-offender-registry information for employment is conceded; the live 12(b)(6) fight is source (NSOR vs Megan's Law website / Exhibit A SOURCE OF RECORD: CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY). They still argue Labor Code 432.7(n) as a safe harbor to restrict employment based on criminal history, plus Gov't Code § 12952 Fair Chance as 'obtained pursuant to procedures otherwise provided for under federal, state, or local law'; they write 432.9(n) then quote 432.7(n). ICRAA is collapsed into the § 290.46(j) theory. They ask dismissal with prejudice. Dkt. 14-1 COS is mail-only to bnn.cdla@gmail.com (wrong extra 'a'; real is bnn.cdl@gmail.com). The only Decisional / INELIGIBLE component is the NSOR hit whose Sentence field reads SOURCE OF RECORD: CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY. Count I is the load-bearing claim; Williams knocks the Tameny label on Count II, not the statutory private right of action. Negligence per se (Count V) is a doctrine, not a COA (Dent). REMAND: not worth filing. UPS's own amount-in-controversy math concedes the point is close — $21/hr x 16 hrs/wk x 179 weeks = $60,144, below the $75,000 threshold, and its ¶34 says a conservative estimate only 'nearly exceeds' it — and its future-attorney's-fee theory for a pro se plaintiff is unsupported by any evidence, contrary to Fritsch v. Swift Transp. Co. of Ariz., LLC, 899 F.3d 785, 794-95 (9th Cir. 2018). But Plaintiff's own July 12, 2026 pre-filing demand of $85,000 is admissible evidence of the amount in controversy under Cohn v. PetSmart, Inc., 281 F.3d 837, 840 (9th Cir. 2002), and the PC §290.46(j)(4)(A) civil penalty (capped at $25,000, plus actual damages, fees, and exemplary damages) stacks on top of the $60,144 wage figure. A remand motion loses and costs a month. UPSIDE OF REMOVAL: Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1) initial disclosures and Rule 45 reach the First Advantage report without a demurrer cycle; UPS has demanded a jury; and a 15 U.S.C. §1681b(b)(3)(A) FCRA claim — already supported by the pre-adverse/final-adverse notices in evidence — is now natively at home here and carries real fee-shifting under §§1681n-1681o, which is the fee theory that actually works for a pro se plaintiff. DOWNSIDE: the Aug. 26 MTD leads with Tameny/Williams and the national-registry construction. Count I does not need a FAC to survive; the opposition is on file as Dkt. 10. A FAC by Sep. 16 is a pleading tool, not a calendar tool. On punitives, the Aug. 17 §425.115 notice sets nothing in federal court; a punitive award still requires evidence of UPS's financial condition (Adams v. Murakami (1991) 54 Cal.3d 105).
